main.title: Bearing-only maritime localization
main.notes: We want to locate a boat from the directions of objects around it. The geographic map supplies possible object locations, but the bearing reports do not identify which catalog entry produced each observation. That makes the problem both geometric and combinatorial. Charleston will provide one recurring scene as we move from the full coast into the harbor and then to individual candidates. The map combines electronic navigational chart features with archived Automatic Identification System positions. Those are real geographic inputs. The observations and observer used for the localization result are simulated. This is a review of the implemented method and one saved experiment, rather than a report of an onboard field deployment. Keeping the same harbor throughout the talk lets us connect every later numerical result to a specific piece of geography.
main.figure_requirements: A large Charleston map crop containing actual shoreline, canonical chart aids and AIS positions. Use the B17 location as an annotated point. A small coast locator provides geographic context.
main.transition: Begin with the size of the location question.
main.asset_plan: F01. New rendering from saved data. Approximately 30 seconds.

main.title: Where is the observer?
main.notes: The left view is the full declared Eastern Seaboard search rectangle. The Charleston inset lets us understand the observation scene, but that crop was not supplied as the position prior in the coast-wide experiment. Initially the observer is hidden so we can distinguish what the search receives from what the evaluator knows. The evaluator later uses the chosen Charleston coordinate to measure error. The solver instead receives the coast-wide catalog, map, bearing frame and search bounds. It must preserve alternatives elsewhere until the positive evidence rules them out. This distinction matters whenever a presentation zooms toward a result. A display crop can improve readability, but it cannot silently reduce the computational search area. The next example motivates why directions can be useful even when object range is uncertain.
main.figure_requirements: Matched full Eastern Seaboard and Charleston views, with the observer’s location initially hidden. Reveal the evaluation location after showing the size of the search domain.
main.transition: Use the actual harbor to motivate uncertain range.
main.asset_plan: F01/F02 alternate views. Approximately 1 minute.

main.title: Range uncertainty
main.notes: Consider the saved Charleston observer and a mapped object along one bearing. Changing an inferred range moves the proposed observer along that same ray. The inset magnifies a calculated plus-or-minus ten-percent range change, corresponding to approximately plus-or-minus 276 projected meters on this geometry. The object positions and ray remain fixed; the displaced observer marks show the range sensitivity. This is a mathematical construction on real mapped coordinates. The search uses bearing constraints and a declared visibility range without accepting measured object ranges as input. Multiple directions then constrain the location jointly. Before combining those directions, we need to state their reference orientation.
main.figure_requirements: Actual Charleston object coordinates with a fixed bearing ray and an along-ray zoom showing the calculated ±276 projected-meter displacement for ±10% range sensitivity. Keep the displaced observer marks inside the inset without moving the actual object coordinates.
main.transition: Define the orientation convention before using bearings.
main.asset_plan: F03. Declared ±10% range-sensitivity calculation on the saved Charleston geometry, with an along-ray magnification. Approximately 1 minute.
main.caption: Calculated ±10% range sensitivity on saved Charleston geometry

main.title: Bearings relative to true north
main.notes: A relative camera direction and a globally referenced bearing are different quantities. Let $\alpha$ be the observer-relative direction and $\psi$ the known heading clockwise from true north. Their sum, wrapped around the circle, gives the global bearing $\beta$. The figure uses the saved Charleston observer and mapped clear Beacon 93428. Its WGS84 azimuth is $\beta = 86.6177095761^\circ$. For this declared calculation, choose $\psi = 30^\circ$; the corresponding relative direction is $\alpha = 56.6177095761^\circ$. The thirty-degree heading is an illustrative input, not a recorded vessel heading. The current measurement file already contains global bearings, so the location solver does not estimate heading as another search dimension. Heading and sensor alignment are upstream assumptions. The true-north and heading rays use geodesically derived endpoints. Their projected angles differ from map-axis directions because grid north and true north differ on this projection.
main.figure_requirements: Use data/heading-demo.json for the saved observer, clear Beacon 93428 bearing, and geodesically derived true-north and heading endpoints. Show the chosen ψ = 30°, relative α = 56.6177095761° and global β = 86.6177095761°. Identify the heading as a declared calculation rather than a recorded heading.
main.transition: Separate directions from object identities.
main.asset_plan: F04. Declared heading conversion using the saved Charleston observer and mapped clear Beacon 93428. Approximately 1.5 minutes.
main.caption: Declared heading-conversion calculation on saved Charleston geometry

main.title: Bearings without supplied object identities
main.notes: The saved input contains 64 positive chart-aid bearings. Each report gives a direction, type and uncertainty information, but it does not carry the correct chart-object identity or range into the search. At a proposed observer position, the catalog predicts several possible objects in similar directions. A valid explanation must associate the reports with compatible distinct physical objects. That is why intersecting a few pre-identified rays would not represent the whole implemented problem. The correspondence lines revealed here come from the saved selected assignment, after the search, rather than from identities supplied to it. The ten-kilometer range remains useful because it bounds which objects might be visible from a candidate. It is a sensor-model limit, not a measured range attached to each observation.
main.figure_requirements: The saved bearing set as a polar display beside the mapped catalog. Initially omit correspondence lines; reveal a few actual final correspondences afterward.
main.transition: Preview the complete input-to-output path.
main.asset_plan: F05. Render saved measurements and selected assignment. Approximately 1 minute.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: The system
main.notes: This is the complete input-to-output relationship. Geographic objects and shoreline geometry define the world. A forward sensor model produces the observation frame. The reverse search asks which observer positions can explain the positive reports, and a declared selector chooses among certified terminal candidates. Two object channels appear in the scene: chart aids and vessels. The current coast-wide result uses only the chart-aid bearing reports as observed localization constraints. AIS-source objects can still affect the physical scene and its angular grouping, but the six observed vessel bearings are not passed into the current deterministic aid objective. A combined observed-vessel-bearing objective remains a proposed evaluation branch. That distinction will remain visible when we discuss results, so the audience does not attribute the reported accuracy to information that the solver did not use.
main.figure_requirements: A flat process diagram built from actual input and output thumbnails. Geographic catalog → simulated bearing frame → spatial search → selected location. Show two observation channels, chart aids and vessels, entering the broader scene model.
main.transition: Establish the geographic source provenance.
main.asset_plan: F06. Code-grounded diagram, not an invented execution trace. Approximately 1 minute.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Geographic data sources
main.notes: The source pages establish where the geographic inputs came from. NOAA electronic navigational charts supply the chart features and shoreline-related geometry. The archived vessel-traffic data supply reported vessel positions. The actual analysis uses saved project archives, rather than fetching changing service responses during the search. The website captures should carry their capture dates, while the notes identify the archive and snapshot dates used by the experiment. This prevents a current screenshot from being mistaken for the original service response. Chart source records also vary in scale and epoch. We retain their metadata and provenance instead of presenting a single universal map resolution or claiming that every source conflict has been reconciled. The next map shows the actual quantity and geographic distribution of those saved objects.
main.figure_requirements: Two tightly cropped official website captures, NOAA ENC Direct and the NOAA/Marine Cadastre vessel-traffic page, next to small examples of the downloaded point/polygon data.
main.transition: Show the distribution of the saved catalog.
main.asset_plan: F07. New documentary screenshots proposed; no new data download needed. Approximately 1 minute.

main.title: The Eastern Seaboard catalog
main.notes: The coast-wide catalog contains 32,168 canonical exact-coordinate chart locations and 2,268 AIS-source records. Together they form the 34,436-object canonical geographic catalog used by the saved experiment. The chart count includes 31,925 locations classified as physical aids and 243 retaining unknown classification. The AIS-source count includes 2,248 normalized vessel rows and 20 rows without a normalized type. Their source identity remains AIS even when classification is unresolved. At this scale, point symbols may require documented display aggregation to remain legible; the local views use the actual positions. These counts describe catalog entries across the declared domain, not objects simultaneously visible from Charleston. We next zoom into the harbor to connect that distribution with the structure available to a bearing-only search.
main.figure_requirements: A large map with chart locations and AIS records as distinguishable shapes. Use a small symbol key and a scale bar.
main.transition: Zoom into the recurring harbor.
main.asset_plan: F08. New rendering from saved geographic archives. Approximately 1 minute.

main.title: Charleston’s mapped objects
main.notes: Charleston provides a more useful view of why the geographic signature is informative. Charted features follow channels, shoreline corners and harbor structures, while the archived AIS positions supply a different spatial pattern. A local inset can expose a busy section without changing its coordinates. Several different counts may be relevant here, and they must stay separate. A map crop contains one set of records; the sensor radius selects a subset; land visibility reduces that subset further; grouping and missed detections then determine the final reports. The displayed local count should therefore be computed for the declared crop and labeled accordingly. Before generating observations, we also need to distinguish physical objects from the multiple chart components that can occupy one exact location.
main.figure_requirements: A generous harbor crop with actual aids and AIS positions. Add an inset of a busy channel or shoreline corner.
main.transition: Resolve chart components before counting physical markers.
main.asset_plan: F10. New saved-data rendering. Approximately 1 minute.

main.title: Three components, one location
main.notes: This particular chart location illustrates the identity preparation directly. The daymark, light and beacon component records have exactly the same latitude and longitude, 32.7731847 and minus 79.9054558. Their source identifiers include daymark 191488, light 206646 and beacon 93433 in chart US5CHSDD.000. The canonicalizer represents that exact coordinate once while retaining the original component records and their attributes. It does not merge nearby coordinates using a distance threshold. This matters because counting every chart component as a distinct visible marker could produce false support for several observations. The resulting canonical object also appears in the final 64-object assignment, so this is part of the actual data path. Across the source catalog, 64,400 component rows become 32,168 exact-coordinate locations.
main.figure_requirements: A tight actual map crop centered at 32.7731847, −79.9054558. Use leader lines to the co-located beacon, light and daymark source records. Reveal their shared canonical location.
main.transition: Establish the independent AIS time snapshot.
main.asset_plan: F11. New rendering of three actual retained source components. Approximately 1.5 minutes.

main.title: The AIS snapshot
main.notes: The AIS inputs come from a one-minute archived window on July 15, 2023, from 12:00 to 12:01 UTC. For each vessel identity, the retained report is the one nearest the midpoint of that window. That gives a position snapshot rather than a measured track for this presentation. We should not infer an observed path or velocity history from a single retained position. The distributed point catalog also omits vessel names and MMSIs. The chart extraction occurred in October 2026, so the physical scene is a mixed-epoch geographic test world rather than a reconstruction of one fully synchronized real harbor moment. This limits how we interpret a future AIS-bearing experiment. For the current result, the observed vessel-bearing channel remains outside the localization objective.
main.figure_requirements: A one-minute time window and the actual selected AIS positions. A small table-like graphic may show multiple source timestamps for one retained record only if those original reports are available.
main.transition: Locate the configured scenarios along the coast.
main.asset_plan: F12. Source-selection diagram and existing position snapshot. Approximately 1 minute.

main.title: Test locations
main.notes: The project defines 24 B locations along the coast. They provide configured viewpoints for creating scenarios, and their stored map status and map hash record the geographic check used when they were chosen. They are not 24 completed accuracy experiments. Charleston is the completed coast-wide localization case discussed in this review. Additional harbor crops can show how channel geometry and object density vary, but displaying a viewpoint does not establish a successful result there. The current CSV should control the displayed coordinates rather than older visibility illustrations. Any new simulated frame for another port needs its own recorded settings, inputs and diagnostic outputs before it can enter the evaluation set. With the map and viewpoints defined, we can now state exactly what the simulator produces.
main.figure_requirements: The 24 B locations over the coast, with a few actual harbor crops arranged geographically.
main.transition: Move from geographic inputs to generated observations.
main.asset_plan: F13. New rendering; current-code multiport simulation recordings proposed. Approximately 1 minute.

main.title: What the simulator produces
main.notes: The two linked views show opposite directions through the problem. In the forward direction, the simulator receives the map, catalog, chosen observer position and sensor configuration. It calculates range and land visibility, combines angularly unresolved objects and applies the configured detection effects. Its output is the observation list. In the reverse direction, the search receives that list and the geographic inputs, while the chosen observer position remains separate. It must infer where the boat could be. The known observer coordinate is retained only so the evaluator can later measure the selected estimate's error. The reports shown here are the exact saved 70-report canonical frame, with 64 aid reports and six vessel reports. They are simulated observations on real geographic geometry. The next slides unpack each forward-model operation.
main.figure_requirements: Two linked views of the same saved Charleston example. On the left, show the virtual boat at its known location on the real map, with mapped objects around it. On the right, show the resulting bearing-only observation frame as a polar display. Use a short reveal from the scene to the measured directions. Omit object identities, measured ranges and the boat coordinate from the search-input display. The extra vessel report is a bearing only and must not be drawn as a geographically located real vessel.
main.transition: Specify the sensor that produced the saved frame.
main.asset_plan: F14. Render the saved canonical scene and its exact 70-report frame. Approximately 1.5 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Sensor configuration
main.notes: The sensor has a full-circle view and a ten-kilometer range limit. Its 0.1-degree angular resolution controls which nearby directions merge into one report. That resolution is separate from bearing noise. The underlying Gaussian noise distribution has standard deviation one-sixth of a degree, and rejection sampling restricts accepted draws to a hard half-degree bound. Detection probability is 0.9, allowing real groups to be missed. Deliberate type errors and the separate bearing-outlier mechanism are both disabled. Additional reports represent vessels only, with a Poisson mean of one. The saved frame contains one such extra report, but that count is a realization rather than a guaranteed count in every frame. The deterministic chart-aid search uses positive detections and applies no penalty when a listed aid is not observed.
main.figure_requirements: A single range-and-angle map with concise numerical labels placed on relevant geometry.
main.transition: Separate radius from visibility.
main.asset_plan: F15. Current protocol and real map. Approximately 1.5 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Visibility range changes the scene
main.notes: These panels filter the same 200 saved in-range physical objects and their recorded line-of-sight statuses at four radius limits. At one kilometer, all six objects are visible. At three kilometers, 45 of 54 are visible; at five kilometers, 70 of 102 are visible; at ten kilometers, 80 of 200 are visible. Each label gives visible objects over objects inside the radius. The panels retain the actual Charleston coordinates and a shared object legend. They show how distance and land blocking jointly change available geometric support. They do not introduce separately simulated detection or noise frames at each radius. The saved localization result uses the ten-kilometer frame. The next pair of rays isolates why land blocks one mapped object while another remains visible.
main.figure_requirements: Matched Charleston maps at 1, 3, 5 and 10 km using the saved 200-object line-of-sight export filtered by range. Label visible/in-range counts 6/6, 45/54, 70/102 and 80/200 with a common object legend and readable lower captions.

main.title: Land blocks sight lines
main.notes: These two examples use actual saved chart coordinates and recorded map-derived visibility. The clear beacon, source object 93428 in US5CHSDD, is 2,749.54 meters from the chosen observer. The blocked beacon, source object 93424 in US5CHSDC, is 7,372.43 meters away. Its saved diagnostic records 2,797.49 meters of raw-land intersection. The two rays should have separate readable panels or bounds that include both actual targets. These are geographic calculations, not measured camera rays. The simulator and final candidate predictor apply the full polygon sight-line calculation. The raw pruning graph uses a deliberately more permissive model and does not yet remove every edge through this complete polygon test. That separation matters later when we interpret unresolved candidates. Visibility reduces the scene, after which angular resolution can reduce the number of reports again.
main.figure_requirements: Two saved Charleston rays in separate panels or shared bounds containing both targets. Clear Beacon US5CHSDD source 93428 at 2.74954 km; blocked Beacon US5CHSDC source 93424 at 7.37243 km. Highlight the saved 2.79749 km land intersection on the blocked ray. Preserve actual coordinates.
main.transition: Separate visibility from angular resolution.
main.asset_plan: F17. Render saved ray records and polygons; no new diagnostic needed. Approximately 1.5 minutes.

main.title: Angular merging
main.notes: The saved canonical scene has 80 clear-visible physical objects but only 79 angular groups. The illustrated pair contains two distinct mapped positions at bearings 343.59362054 and 343.68509401 degrees. Their separation is 0.09147347 degrees, below the configured 0.1-degree grouping threshold. Their ranges are approximately 2.036 and 4.433 kilometers, so the nearer object supplies the representative bearing and type. This pair produced saved observation index 58, using zero-based indexing. The map preserves both actual coordinates, while the angular inset magnifies their directional separation. Circular angular grouping also handles adjacent directions across the zero-degree wrap. This differs from exact-coordinate canonicalization, which resolves multiple chart components at one location. Angular merging instead describes distinct visible objects that the sensor cannot resolve in direction. The representative then receives the bounded sensor error described next.
main.figure_requirements: Show the actual pair for saved observation index 58 (zero-based) at bearings 343.59362054° and 343.68509401°, separated by 0.09147347°. Mark ranges 2.036 km and 4.433 km and identify the nearer representative. Preserve actual coordinates and use a magnified angular inset with distinct endpoint callouts.
main.transition: Add the declared bearing error to the representative direction.
main.asset_plan: F18. Saved group diagnostic and canonical coordinates. Approximately 1.5 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Bounded angular noise
main.notes: The histogram contains the recovered bearing errors of the 69 detected physical groups in this exact saved Charleston frame. The additional vessel report is not a noisy observation of a physical target, so it is excluded from this histogram. The largest recovered absolute error is approximately 0.392584 degrees, within the configured half-degree bound. The generating distribution is Gaussian with underlying standard deviation one-sixth of a degree, rejection-sampled inside that bound. The histogram describes simulated draws on real geographic objects; it is not a distribution measured by an onboard sensor. The map wedge gives geometric intuition. At five kilometers, a half-degree deviation corresponds to approximately 43.6 meters of lateral displacement. That is a sensitivity calculation, not the selected localization error. Multiple bearings from distinct objects constrain the observer jointly.

Add one saved-bearing map wedge. Do not include the extra bearing-only vessel report in the error histogram.

main.title: Worked harbor examples
main.notes: Harbor geometry varies, so the same sensor settings need not produce equally informative scenes at every port. A shared-scale view of Charleston, Norfolk and Portland can show real differences in channels, shoreline layout and catalog object density. Those geographic panels can be drawn from existing archives. However, report bearings and report counts should appear only for frames actually recorded with the current simulator. The other port frames and their diagnostic exports remain proposed work. Their appearance in a map strip must not imply completed coast-wide accuracy evaluations from all three locations. Future comparisons should preserve their geographic versions, observer choices, seeds and sensor assumptions so the scenes form a declared evaluation set. We now turn from forward-model examples to the search's required logical statement.
main.figure_requirements: A shared-scale strip of Charleston, Norfolk and Portland, with real shoreline, aids and AIS. Reveal simulated bearing reports only for examples recorded with the current simulator.
main.transition: State the mathematical compatibility requirement.
main.asset_plan: F21. Charleston saved data plus proposed recordings for additional ports. Approximately 2 minutes.

main.title: What the search must establish
main.notes: Let the observer position be $x$, a mapped object position be $q_j$ and a positive report be $\theta_i$ with hard tolerance $\epsilon_i$. The predicted global direction is the WGS84 azimuth from $x$ to $q_j$. At a single candidate point, range, visibility and the wrapped bearing residual define possible explanations. The assignment must be injective because distinct trusted marker detections require distinct physical objects. For a whole cell $C$, the incidence graph must include every explanation that could hold anywhere within that cell. This graph deliberately permits extra possibilities when a bound or visibility condition is uncertain. If even that expanded graph cannot support all reports, the entire cell is impossible. A successful graph match is only a necessary condition; it does not itself certify a final position.
main.figure_requirements: One mathematical formulation with a real-map thumbnail. Observed bearings are matched injectively to possible chart objects at a candidate position.
main.transition: Calculate the cost of checking every fine location.
main.asset_plan: F22. Mathematics and actual map context. Approximately 2 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Exhaustive search, even across multiple GPUs
main.notes: The declared projected rectangle is about 1,644,676 meters wide and 2,388,459 meters high. A calculated one-meter grid therefore contains approximately 3.93 trillion positions. Even a simplified budget of 64 report checks per position already implies about 251 trillion checks, before association and visibility are considered. Dividing the positions perfectly among three GPUs still leaves about 1.31 trillion positions for each device. This is arithmetic on the real bounds, not a benchmark. Multiple devices divide work; pruning changes how much work remains. The current implementation uses GPUs zero through two for the numerical search, while CPU coordination launches work and writes outputs. We do not infer days of brute-force runtime from an unmeasured throughput. The next slide shows how whole-region reasoning avoids visiting most of those fine locations.
main.figure_requirements: The actual projected search rectangle with its dimensions and calculated grid count, followed by an ideal division across three GPU lanes. Keep a small current-method annotation that the recorded search uses GPUs 0–2. This is a work-budget diagram, not a measured brute-force experiment.
main.transition: Replace exhaustive point enumeration with hierarchical regions.
main.asset_plan: F23. Derived calculation on actual bounds and the recorded three-device configuration. Approximately 2 minutes.

main.title: Coarse-to-fine search
main.notes: The search starts with ten-kilometer root cells and subdivides every surviving cell into four children. It stops when a cell's maximum width is at most one meter. Under this dyadic schedule the nominal full-cell width reaches approximately 0.61035 meters after 14 halvings. There is no fixed top-N shortlist or random initial location sample. That preserves coverage, but subdivision alone does not reduce work. An unpruned tree would be enormous. The advantage comes from rejecting a coarse cell with a sound proof, which removes all of its descendants at once. The illustrated cell is an actual geographic region, while the subdivision overlay is mathematical unless it is tied to a recorded traversal. We next separate the predicates that can establish such a rejection from conditions that only leave a location unresolved.
main.figure_requirements: One actual geographic cell subdivided into four children, with the bearing-support envelope narrowing over successive scales. Use one fixed real catalog object.
main.transition: Identify which evidence can reject a region.
main.asset_plan: F24. Mathematical subdivision of a real cell, clearly distinguished from a recorded survivor trajectory. Approximately 2 minutes.

main.title: Pruning
main.notes: A positive chart-aid detection asserts an existing object. The four conditions shown can reject an entire candidate cell. The cell may be entirely known land, a report may have no possible object, there may be too few distinct possibilities, or no simultaneous injective assignment may exist. Missing a mapped aid never creates a penalty. The approved pruning-only recording captured every decision using the current GPU predicate. It contains 5,931 land rejections,39,011 individual-support rejections,475 distinct-count rejections and 12,701 injective-matching rejections. Their sum is 58,118. Unknown geometry cannot remove a possible explanation without a valid proof. The next slide shows an actual recorded matching rejection rather than a constructed adjacency example.
main.figure_requirements: Actual recorded cells demonstrating known land, a report with no possible object, and insufficient distinct possible objects. Use modest captions and actual candidate bounds.
main.transition: Move from individual support to simultaneous distinct support.
main.asset_plan: F25. Proposed current-run decision recording. Approximately 2 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Distinct markers must explain distinct reports
main.notes: This graph is extracted from a real rejected cell in the approved coast-wide pruning recording. Reports 38,39 and 40 use zero-based order within the 64 positive aid reports. Every one of these three reports can be explained individually. However, their complete combined neighborhood contains only two canonical catalog entries. All six possible edges for this subset are drawn. Three distinct reports cannot be assigned to only two objects, so the entire candidate cell is rejected. The displayed object labels $q_0$ and $q_1$ are local drawing indices. They refer to snapshot columns 867 and 868, catalog rows 14232 and 14231; their complete canonical keys and supplied positions are preserved in the witness JSON. The full cell graph contains 1,359 candidate objects. The failure comes from the subset relationship, rather than a shortage in that overall count. Both graph flags and proof validity were checked in the recorded GPU output. The CPU extracted the explanatory subset afterward from saved adjacency; it did not decide search pruning. This is a recorded example of the Hall condition. The next slide distinguishes this conservative cell proof from final point scoring.
main.figure_requirements: A map crop and its actual recorded report-to-object incidence graph. Highlight a deficient subset and then a retained injective explanation from another recorded cell.
main.transition: Distinguish impossibility from retained uncertainty.
main.asset_plan: F26. Proposed incidence-graph capture during the current-code recording. Approximately 2 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: Deterministic marker scoring
main.notes: After conservative pruning, deterministic point scoring asks whether a center has a complete explanation for all 64 positive marker reports. The assignment must be injective, so distinct reports use distinct physical markers. Every selected wrapped bearing residual must satisfy the hard half-degree tolerance, including the numerical margin required by the implementation. A certified consistent center also requires zero numerical flags, known water at the observer, and certified visibility and grouping for the matched support. Unmatched catalog objects are not penalized because missing detections are allowed. The selector considers consistent centers with complete assignments and minimizes the sum of wrapped absolute bearing residuals. The selected Charleston center has a sum of 6.2809796 degrees across 64 matches; this is not a mean. Fixed east-then-north tie-breaking makes selection deterministic. The estimate is saved and hashed before the separate evaluator reads simulated truth. The conservative proof behavior and retained unresolved centers remain distinct from this ranking step.
main.figure_requirements: Current figure plan. Display deterministic point scoring with wrapped absolute residuals, injective 64-of-64 marker matching, hard ±0.5° acceptance, zero flags, known observer water and certified matched visibility/grouping. Identify 6.2809796° as the selected summed residual. This aligns the explanation with the existing residual diagram and changes no algorithm.
main.transition: Follow the full search from the coast into the surviving harbor region.
main.asset_plan: F27. Existing deterministic residual diagram aligned with the current saved scoring and selection semantics. Approximately 1.5 minutes.
main.caption: Simulated observations on NOAA geometry

main.title: The coast-wide search contracts toward Charleston
main.notes: The video shows the approved recording of every current pruning decision. It begins with all 39,435 root cells. The first 10 km pruning retains 851 and rejects 38,584. Subsequent frames group actual decisions by generation through 14 halvings; the ending cell width is 0.6103515625 m. Retained cell counts can increase when one region is replaced by four children. That count increase does not mean a larger candidate area. The fixed left panel keeps all surviving coastal regions visible. The right panel begins as a Charleston reference crop and zooms to all remaining regions once their global bounds fit in that harbor view. Earlier masks come from the recorded decisions, never from ancestors reconstructed only from final survivors. The trace contains 64,875 evaluated regions,58,118 rejections and 6,360 expansions, leaving 397 terminal rectangles. All recorded roots and four-child expansions were checked, and the final 397 rectangles are bitwise identical to the saved timed run. The final classification overlay comes from that frozen run and shows 148 consistent,67 inconsistent and 182 unresolved centers. Terminal scoring was not rerun. Playback is scale-ordered for explanation rather than the chronological interleaving of three GPUs. Recording overhead and playback duration do not replace the 8.46 second search measurement. The following slide accounts for the entire traversal.

backup.notes: A whole-cell rejection must hold for every possible observer position in the cell and every object position allowed by its support bound.
